high_priority_articles.full_text:
The EU will soon add over 1,600 names, including 77 lawmakers who stood for election in the occupied territories of Ukraine, to its Russia sanctions. The decision comes amid an unsettling rise in hybrid attacks.
The European Union has agreed the single largest expansion of its sanctions list against Russia, adding 1,646 names in one go.
The deal, sealed on Wednesday by ambassadors in Brussels, covers 743 individuals and 826 entities accused of supporting Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Separately, it targets 77 lawmakers who stood in the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine for the widely discredited State Duma election in September.
Ambassadors wrapped up the agreement after several weeks of deliberations and legal scrubbing, which was particularly intensive given the sheer number of names.
It will be formally approved on Monday when foreign ministers gather in Luxembourg. The targeted people and entities will then be made public.
Sanctions entail a travel ban, an asset freeze and a prohibition on providing funding.
Member states were keen to close the agreement to portray a united front amid a rapid succession of hybrid attacks, some attributed to Russia. Work has already begun on new listings in response to the drone incident at the Leipzig airport in Germany.
Another reason to project unity is last month's contentious decision to remove two high-profile oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the blacklist.
Usmanov's removal, at France's request, was tied to a prisoner release with Azerbaijan brokered by the Turkic states, which have long lobbied in the billionaire's favour. One French citizen has been released while a second remains in prison.
In exchange for the painful concession, the EU extended the sanctions list for an unprecedented three years. In total, the blacklist will soon cover almost 4,650 names.
Earlier this week, High Representative Kaja Kallas celebrated the three-year renewal but admitted it is unlikely that Usmanov and Fridman will be included again.
"Countries are free to put forward names that should be included in the sanctions list. But in the end, it is up to the member states to decide," Kallas said.
"And I do not see this on these two persons happening any time soon."
Brussels is still grappling with the aftermath of the Usmanov saga and the precedent it might have set for the common foreign policy, which relies on unanimity.
As the bloc prepares to admit new members, the European Commission has proposed using the so-called passerelle clause to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting on issues such as sanctions, thereby avoiding the multiplication of vetoes.
But the clause creates a textbook Catch-22: it requires unanimity to end unanimity.

Eastport Critical Metals CEO Daniel Major joined Steve Darling from Proactive to discuss the company’s diversified critical minerals portfolio in Botswana, recent rare earth drilling results and plans to advance its uranium, copper and nickel projects through 2026 and into 2027.
Major highlighted Botswana’s established mining industry, infrastructure and government support for mineral development. Eastport Critical Metals has six projects covering five commodities, with its portfolio focused on minerals that could benefit from growing global electrification and demand for critical raw materials.
A major focus is the company’s large-scale uranium project in northern Botswana, where an exploration target covering almost 300 square kilometres has been identified. Gravity surveys and additional geophysical work are underway to refine targets ahead of a drilling programme expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.
The company is also advancing its rare earth project near Gaborone, where recent drilling returned an intersection exceeding 330 metres at 0.21% rare earths. Major said further assay results are pending as Eastport evaluates the scale and continuity of the mineralization and determines the next phase of exploration.
At its nickel-copper project near the Selebi mine, soil sampling has identified correlations between nickel-copper anomalies and the underlying geology. Eastport plans to conduct additional electromagnetic surveys to help define potential drilling targets.
Major said the company is continuing to evaluate opportunities across its broader portfolio while prioritizing its larger-scale projects. Depending on the development requirements of individual assets, potential strategies could include joint ventures, asset sales or spinning projects into separate companies.
Looking ahead, Major pointed to growing interest in rare earths and copper from both companies and governments, while also highlighting the potential for renewed investor attention toward uranium as global demand for critical minerals continues to grow.
Eastport’s diversified approach is designed to give the company exposure to multiple critical mineral markets while allowing it to advance projects according to their individual exploration and development potential.

high_priority_articles.summary: Malaysia to work towards Myanmar's full reintegration into ASEAN, PM says  Yahoo News Singapore
high_priority_articles.full_text:
By Rozanna Latiff and Hasnoor Hussain
KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Malaysia hosted Myanmar's junta chief-turned-President Min Aung Hlaing on Thursday, saying it aimed to reintegrate the country with Southeast Asian bloc ASEAN, but made clear the visit did not amount to recognition for the military-backed government.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim pledged to continue working with Myanmar on tasks such as the repatriation of thousands of its nationals, a move criticised by the United Nations and rights groups concerned about the risks stemming from civil war.
"Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we ... ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN," Anwar told media after meeting Min Aung Hlaing.
The Myanmar leader's two-day visit aims to build greater international legitimacy after Min Aung Hlaing became president in April following an election criticised as a sham by rights groups and Western nations.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since 2021, when Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup against a democratically elected government, unleashing armed conflict across much of the country.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations barred Min Aung Hlaing and senior Myanmar officials from its summits for not adhering to an ASEAN-brokered peace plan after the coup.
But some member nations, such as Cambodia, Laos, Thailandand Vietnam, have sought to re-establish ties.
Anwar acknowledged concerns about Myanmar's democratic processes but called for differences to be respected, adding that Min Aung Hlaing had shown willingness to be collaborative.
Malaysian government spokesperson Fahmi Fadzil denied that Min Aung Hlaing's visit amounted to recognition of Myanmar's government, however, state news agency Bernama said.
"This meeting does not mean we recognise the Myanmar government," Fahmi, who is communications minister, was quoted as saying. "It is intended to find a solution to the long-standing issue of Myanmar refugees in our country."
MYANMAR TO SEND MORE NAVY SHIPS TO REPATRIATE ITS CITIZENS
Anwar also expressed appreciation to Min Aung Hlaing for accepting the return home of 10,493 Myanmar nationals from Malaysia.
Malaysia has said it can no longer take in refugees from Myanmar, citing the financial burden and security risk. As it is not a party to the UN refugee convention, Malaysia treats asylum-seekers as illegal migrants.
Last month it sent back about 1,500 people on Myanmar naval ships, part of a wider repatriation effort to deport as many as 5,000.
Myanmar citizens held in Malaysian immigration centres would be taken home as soon as possible, Min Aung Hlaing said.
"Because the current weather is favourable, I will dispatch navy ships to repatriate them," he told Thursday's briefing,
adding that he would invite Anwar to visit when the time was right.
The leaders did not say if their talks covered repatriation plans for Rohingya Muslim refugees, many of whom fled Myanmar after a brutal 2017 military crackdown in western Rakhine state.
Muslim-majority Malaysia widely criticised the crackdown at the time. But public sentiment has turned in recent years, with increasing harassment and scrutiny of Rohingya in Malaysia amid a surge of online hate speech and misinformation.
Anwar has said he would push for Myanmar to accept Rohingya refugees. Malaysia was hosting about 193,000 refugees and asylum seekers from Myanmar as of February, about 65% of them Rohingya, UN data shows.
Buddhist-majority Myanmar does not recognise the Rohingya as one of its official ethnic groups and denies citizenship to most.
ASEAN URGED NOT TO LEGITIMISE MYANMAR LEADER
Myanmar's pro-democracy activists and resistance groups have repeatedly urged ASEAN to refrain from conferring political legitimacy on Min Aung Hlaing's presidency.
"His legitimacy is a nightmare for the whole nation, for the people who have ... sacrificed their homes," Swam Saung, a member of the Myanmar Affairs Alliance, told a gathering in Kuala Lumpur, the capital.
He also expressed fear for those repatriated, saying they could face forced conscription in the military conflict with ethnic armed groups.
Malaysia has traditionally upheld principles of humanitarian values, democracy, and human rights during engagements on Myanmar within ASEAN, an umbrella group of Myanmar armed ethnic groups and democratic bodies said.
"Hosting of Min Aung Hlaing at the head-of-state level stands in direct contradiction to these established principles,"
the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union, added in a statement.
(Reporting by Rozanna Latiff and Reuters staff; Additional reporting by Hasnoor Hussain and Ahmad Luqman Ismail; Editing by Kate Mayberry, Raju Gopalakrishnan and Clarence Fernandez)

high_priority_articles.title: Syria mulls military aid to Saudi Arabia as Houthis escalate war
high_priority_articles.summary: Syria is weighing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia, U.S. and Syrian officials said, as the Iran-aligned Houthis step up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom that ki...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Syria is weighing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia, U.S. and Syrian officials said, as the Iran-aligned Houthis step up missile and drone attacks on the kingdom that killed three people at Saudi airports this week.
The possible entry of Syrian forces into the battle, a spillover of the US-Iran conflict, shows how Yemen's reignited civil war has added new chaos to a region already aflame and risks drawing regional states into grueling mountain fighting.
Saudi Arabia has pushed for support from allied nations, including Türkiye and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or purely defensive capacity, an effort made more urgent by the Houthi strikes on its infrastructure such as this week's deadly airport attacks.
A succession of loud booms were reported in Riyadh Thursday morning. There was no immediate official comment and no public early warning alerts, although some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh warned parents of shelter in place orders, according to Reuters.
Yemen's Houthi rebels, however, claimed Thursday that it had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile. The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
One person had been killed in a strike on Riyadh airport and two others in an attack on Abha airport in the southwest Tuesday and Wednesday, Saudi Arabia said late Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and Syrian officials said Damascus was carefully considering military support, including the option of defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks or deployment in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops take the fight to the Houthis.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a cease-fire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
The group's threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and its targeting of Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian Foreign Ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's 14-year civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait as they push to reverse the Houthis' gains of last month.
However, in a messy war with several frontlines, the Houthis have also made some gains of their own this week, surrounding the country's third-largest city of Taiz by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed the Mecca pact with Türkiye and Pakistan, committing all three countries to come to each other's defense, though Ankara still needs to ratify the treaty internally.
NATO-member Türkiye said Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis, and a Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Pakistan, meanwhile, has flown cargo planes of military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said and has deployed troops inside Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom's borders.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Synopsis
The ECB may raise interest rates further as inflation risks remain tilted upward, with rates already at 2.5% and inflation at 3.8%. Policymaker Primoz Dolenc cited energy, food and geopolitical risks, while noting stable core inflation. Strong economic growth could add pressure, but rising bond yields pose risks to euro zone activity.
The ECB has raised its deposit rate twice this year to 2.5% as inflation accelerated to 3.8% last month, nearly twice the central bank's 2% target. Policymakers are assessing whether higher energy costs linked to the Iran war could become embedded more broadly in the euro zone economy.
According to Reuters, however, the composition of recent inflation data offers some reassurance. The latest increase was largely driven by energy prices, while core inflation has remained relatively stable, indicating limited spillover into services and other underlying components.
Inflation risks remain skewed higher
Dolenc said the risks to the inflation outlook remained tilted towards higher prices, particularly because of uncertainty surrounding energy markets.
European gas storage levels ahead of winter are a concern, with any renewed increase in wholesale gas prices potentially passing through to consumers relatively quickly. Food prices could also come under pressure from elevated input costs, drought conditions and the effects of El Niño.
The euro zone's stronger-than-expected economic performance is another potential source of inflationary pressure. The region's economy expanded at its fastest pace in four years in the second quarter, despite expectations that the energy shock would significantly weigh on growth.
Dolenc said the resilience was supported by household consumption and services spending, suggesting that economic activity could remain relatively firm. Survey indicators also point to continued strength.
Rising bond yields a growth risk
Higher longer-term borrowing costs have emerged as a potential downside risk to growth. ECB Executive Board members Philip Lane and Isabel Schnabel have warned that rising yields could weigh on economic activity more than previously anticipated.
Investors have been particularly concerned about the rising premium demanded to hold French government debt, prompting debate over whether the ECB could eventually intervene in bond markets.
According to Reuters, his comments suggest that policymakers remain focused on ensuring that higher borrowing costs do not create financial fragmentation, while continuing to assess whether further rate increases are necessary to bring inflation sustainably back towards the ECB's target.

AGENCY:
United States International Trade Commission.
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
The Commission hereby gives notice of the scheduling of full reviews pursuant to the Tariff Act of 1930 to determine whether revocation of the antidumping duty orders on seamless carbon and alloy steel standard, line, and pressure pipe from Russia and South Korea and countervailing duty orders on seamless carbon and alloy steel standard, line, and pressure pipe from Czechia, Russia, South Korea, and Ukraine would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury within a reasonably foreseeable time. The Commission has determined to exercise its authority to extend the review period by up to 90 days.
DATES:
October 5, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Laurel Schwartz (202-205-2398), Office of Investigations, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436. Hearing-impaired persons can obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on 202-205-1810. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at 202-205-2000. General information concerning the Commission may also be obtained by accessing its internet server (
https://www.usitc.gov). The public record for this review may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at
https://edis.usitc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background.
—On June 5, 2026, the Commission determined that responses to its notice of institution of the subject five-year review were such that a full review should proceed (91 FR 50894, August 6, 2026); accordingly, a full review is being scheduled pursuant to section 751(c)(5) of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1675(c)(5)). A record of the Commissioners' votes, the Commission's statement on adequacy, and any individual Commissioner's statements are available from the Office of the Secretary and at the Commission's website.
Participation in the review and public service list.
—Persons, including industrial users of the subject merchandise and, if the merchandise is sold at the retail level, representative consumer organizations, wishing to participate in this review as parties must file an entry of appearance with the Secretary to the Commission, as provided in section 201.11 of the Commission's rules, by 45 days after publication of this notice. A party that filed a notice of appearance following publication of the Commission's notice of institution of the review need not file an additional notice of appearance. The Secretary will maintain a public service list containing the names and addresses of all persons, or their representatives, who are parties to the review.
For further information concerning the conduct of this review and rules of general application, consult the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure, part 201, subparts A and B (19 CFR part 201), and part 207, subparts A, D, E, and F (19 CFR part 207).
Please note the Secretary's Office will accept only electronic filings during this time. Filings must be made through the Commission's Electronic Document Information System (EDIS,
https://edis.usitc.gov). No in-person paper-based filings or paper copies of any electronic filings will be accepted until further notice.
Limited disclosure of business proprietary information (BPI) under an administrative protective order (APO) and BPI service list.
—Pursuant to section 207.7(a) of the Commission's rules, the Secretary will make BPI gathered in this review available to authorized applicants under the APO issued in the review, provided that the application is made by 45 days after publication of this notice. Authorized applicants must represent interested parties, as defined by 19 U.S.C. 1677(9), who are parties to the review. A party granted access to BPI following publication of the Commission's notice of institution of the review need not reapply for such access. A separate service list will be maintained by the Secretary for those parties authorized to receive BPI under the APO.
Staff report.
—The prehearing staff report in the review will be placed in the nonpublic record on February 18, 2027, and a public version will be issued thereafter, pursuant to section 207.64 of the Commission's rules.
Hearing.
—The Commission will hold an in-person hearing in connection with the review beginning at 9:30 a.m. on Thursday, March 11, 2027. Requests to appear at the hearing should be filed in writing with the Secretary to the Commission on or before 5:15 p.m. on Wednesday, March 3, 2027. Any requests to appear as a witness via videoconference must be included with your request to appear. Requests to appear via videoconference must include a statement explaining why the witness cannot appear in person; the Chairman, or other person designated to conduct the review, may in their discretion for good cause shown, grant such a request. Requests to appear as remote witness due to illness or a positive COVID-19 test result may be submitted by 3 p.m. the business day prior to the hearing. Further information about participation in the hearing will be posted on the Commission's website at
https://www.usitc.gov/calendarpad/calendar.html.
A nonparty who has testimony that may aid the Commission's deliberations may request permission to present a short statement at the hearing. All parties and nonparties desiring to appear at the hearing and make oral presentations should attend a prehearing conference, if deemed necessary, to be held at 9:30 a.m. on Friday, March 5, 2027. Parties shall file and serve written testimony and presentation slides in connection with their presentation at the hearing by no later than noon on March 10, 2027. Oral testimony and written materials to be submitted at the public hearing are governed by sections 201.6(b)(2), 201.13(f), and 207.24 of the Commission's rules. Parties must submit any request to present a portion of their hearing testimony
in camera

Written submissions.

Parties shall also file written testimony in connection with their presentation at the hearing, and posthearing briefs, which must conform with the provisions of section 207.67 of the Commission's rules. AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that countervailable subsidies were provided to producers and exporters of certain corrosion-resistant steel products (CORE) from the Republic of Korea (Korea), during the period of review (POR) January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review with respect to Dongkuk Coated Metal Co., Ltd (Dongkuk CM). Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable October 8, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Henry Wolfe, AD/CVD Operations, Office VIII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0574.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On July 25, 2016, Commerce published a countervailing duty (CVD) order on CORE from Korea.[1]
On August 22, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), Commerce initiated an administrative review of the
Order.[2]
On September 30, 2025, Commerce selected Hyundai Steel Company (Hyundai Steel) and KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd (KG Dongbu Steel) as the mandatory respondents in this review.[3]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[4]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[5]
On May 14, 2026, we extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review until September 30, 2026.[6]
On September 25, 2026, we extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review an additional five days.[7]
Accordingly, the deadline for these preliminary results is now October 5, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[8]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is provided in Appendix I. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
The product covered by the
Order
is CORE from Korea. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Recission of Administrative Review, In Part
In accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if all parties that requested the review withdraw their requests within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation of the requested review. Commerce received a timely-filed withdrawal request with respect to Dongkuk CM. Because the withdrawal request was timely filed, and no other parties requested a review of this
( printed page 64354)
company, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), Commerce is rescinding this review of the
Order
with respect to Dongkuk CM.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each of the subsidy programs found countervailable, Commerce preliminarily determines that there is a subsidy,
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.[9]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our preliminary results,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rate for Non-Individually Examined Companies
The Act does not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(e)(2) of the Act. However, Commerce's regulation at 19 CFR 351.109(g) states that Commerce will determine the rate for non-selected companies by following the process set forth in 19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)-(2), which generally parallels the process for determining the all-others rate in an investigation under section 705(c)(5) of the Act. Section 705(c)(5)(A) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.109(f) state that for companies not investigated, in general, we will determine an all-others rate by weight averaging the countervailable subsidy rates established for each of the companies individually investigated, excluding zero and
de minimis
rates or any rates based entirely on facts available.
Accordingly, to determine the rate for companies not selected for individual examination, Commerce's practice is to weight-average the net subsidy rates for the selected mandatory respondents, excluding rates that are zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available.[10]
In this administrative review, we preliminarily calculated countervailable subsidy rates for the mandatory respondents, Hyundai Steel and KG Dongbu Steel, that are not zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available. Accordingly, we are preliminarily assigning to the companies under review that were not selected for individual examination a countervailable subsidy rate equal to the weighted average of the countervailable subsidy rates calculated for Hyundai Steel and KG Dongbu Steel, weighted by the mandatory respondents' publicly ranged sales values for the merchandise under consideration, consistent with the guidance in section 705(c)(5)(A)(i) of the Act.[11]

high_priority_articles.title: Still QT plus Renewed Rate Hikes at the ECB despite Surging Bond Yields in the Euro Area - Wolf Street
high_priority_articles.summary: Still QT plus Renewed Rate Hikes at the ECB despite Surging Bond Yields in the Euro Area  Wolf Street
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The ECB shed €95 billion of QE Bonds & Loans in Q3. Since mid-2022, QE assets dropped by 53%! Gold got marked up to market.
By Wolf Richter for WOLF STREET.
Despite surging yields of government bonds in the Euro Area, the ECB shed €95 billion ($106 billion) of its QE bonds and loans in Q3, bringing them down to €3.37 trillion. Since the peak of those QE assets in mid-2022, the ECB has now shed 53%, or €3.79 trillion ($4.25 trillion), of its QE assets.
Let that sink in for a moment. This is an extreme turn for a central bank that had been uber-dovish for over a decade, with negative interest rates and “whatever it takes” QE – the immortal phrase of then ECB president Mario Draghi in 2012 – that lasted from the Euro Debt Crisis through 2022.
Shedding 53% of its QE assets is far more than anyone thought the erstwhile uber-dovish ECB, or any other central bank, could ever shed. The ECB has cleared out nearly all of its mega-sized pandemic-QE!
The bond market has been on its own, slowly re-learning what a bond market is supposed to do, which, it turns out, is not to provide unlimited free private-sector money to governments to fund their ballooning deficits, but to price the risks of inflation, default, and other issues, while funding governments and providing adequate returns for bondholders who take those risks.
Government bond yields have surged since central banks began to reverse QE and hike their policy rates – even the Bank of Japan flipped from QE and Yield Curve Control to QT and has shed 17% of its assets. The threat is a surge of inflation, and for Japan, it’s also the collapse of the yen.
The ECB also re-hiked its policy rates twice by 25 basis points each time, first on June 11 and then again on September 10, lifting its main deposit rate to 2.50%.
By continuing with the balance sheet reduction, and by hiking its policy rates, the ECB is pursuing a clear tightening strategy.
The ECB’s two QE assets: Loans and bonds.
The ECB’s QE consisted of two methods, loans and bonds. Combined, they ballooned from €440 billion in 2012 when Draghi still reigned over the ECB, to €7.16 trillion by mid-2022 at the peak.
The bonds that the ECB acquired during QE were mostly government bonds from the member states, but also included corporate bonds, mortgage bonds, and asset-backed securities that the ECB bought under various programs.
Since mid-2022, when QT began, the ECB:
- Shed 98% of all its loans, bringing them down from €2.2 trillion at the peak to $38 billion (blue in the chart below).
- Shed 33% of its bonds, from €4.96 trillion at the peak to €3.33 trillion now. Bonds come off the balance sheet when they mature and the ECB gets its money back (red).
The ECB has exited the bond market. And nothing bad has happened. Yields have risen back into the pre-QE normal range, and that’s where they should be in a normal bond market. Despite all the brouhaha in France and the hand-wringing about the French 10-year yield, it’s still below 5%. It’s just that everyone misses the free money.
The ECB marked up its gold holdings.
The consolidated balance sheet represents the combined assets, liabilities, and capital of the individual central banks of the Euro Area’s member countries. The German Bundesbank is by far the largest, and also has the largest gold holdings, which account for about 31% of the ECB’s gold and gold receivables.
The ECB marks gold holdings to market prices at the end of every quarter, a somewhat unusual practice among central banks.
On today’s balance sheet, which reflects the value of gold as of September 30, the ECB wrote up its gold holdings by €53 billion, to €1.29 trillion, as the price of gold rose in the July through September period.
In Q2, the ECB had written down its gold holdings by $160 billion, as the price of gold had dropped in the April through June period.
These mark-to-market adjustments are paper adjustments after the end of the quarter and do not involve purchases or sales of gold, money printing, QE or QT. They simply reflect variations in the market price of gold. Neither the Fed nor the BOJ mark their gold and gold receivables to market.
All combined, total assets dropped by €35 billion in Q3, after the €53 billion mark-to-market write-up of its gold holdings, to €5.95 trillion. Without the mark-to-market accounting adjustment of gold, total assets dropped by €88 billion.
In terms of total assets, the huge mark-to-market write-up of its gold in prior years, especially when gold prices exploded in 2025 and Q1 2026, masked a substantial portion of the magnitude of QT. The up-jags in 2025 and 2026 were the effects to the mark-to-market accounting write-ups of gold, amid massive gold price increases, overpowering the amount of the QT runoff.

high_priority_articles.title: Europe’s far-right surge threatens rearmament as Nato spending and Ukraine aid face political test - The Korea Post
high_priority_articles.summary: Europe’s far-right surge threatens rearmament as Nato spending and Ukraine aid face political test  The Korea Post
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Europe’s drive to boost military spending in response to the long-term threat posed by Russia is facing a growing challenge — not from the battlefield, but from the rising cost of living. Far-right parties are capitalising on public frustration over inflation, taxes, pensions and household bills, portraying increased defence spending and support for Ukraine as competing with domestic welfare priorities. Their growing political influence has raised concerns that Europe’s changing political landscape could undermine Nato’s long-term commitment to spend 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence and security by 2035.
According to Politico Europe on 7 October, far-right and nationalist parties gaining ground in France, Italy and Germany are increasingly channelling voters’ concerns about living costs into opposition to higher military spending, assistance for Ukraine and a greater European Union role in defence. Their positions, however, are far from uniform. Some are seeking to curb support for Kyiv, others oppose expanding EU powers over defence policy, while certain parties question the overall increase in military expenditure.
In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has proposed cutting approximately €8bn from the government's original defence spending plans amid pressure from her far-right coalition partner, the League. Claudio Borghi, a senator from the League, has argued that the government cannot justify spending more on weapons when resources are already stretched by pensions, fuel tax cuts and household utility bills. Speaking recently to Italian media, Borghi maintained that prioritising arms expenditure over pensions and energy costs would be an inefficient use of public funds.
Roberto Vannacci, leader of Future National, a far-right party challenging Meloni from the right, has also called for a reassessment of military expenditure. Citing what he described as record-high raw material prices, he has questioned whether this is an appropriate time to increase defence spending.
In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has strengthened its political position following recent state elections, opposes the federal government's plans for a substantial increase in military spending. The party has also called for an end to military assistance to Ukraine and the restoration of relations with Russia, putting it at odds with Berlin's policy towards Moscow. Elsewhere, Poland's nationalist opposition party Law and Justice (PiS) and the Dutch Party for Freedom (PVV) have resisted EU-led defence initiatives and further European defence integration. In Poland, President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has previously blocked an EU defence loan scheme.
Public opinion suggests that European governments cannot assume unconditional support for rearmament. An August survey analysed by the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) found that an average of 46.2% of respondents across eight countries — Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, the Netherlands, Sweden and the United Kingdom — would not support higher defence spending if it meant increased taxes. Opposition to tax rises to fund military expenditure was particularly strong in Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland, where opponents outnumbered supporters. Demonstrations against higher military spending have also taken place this year in Rome, Brussels and Madrid.
Support for Ukraine is also showing signs of political fatigue. Last month, Marine Le Pen of France's far-right National Rally (RN) called for financial assistance to Ukraine to be reduced, arguing that France could no longer afford to maintain support at existing levels. Her position, however, does not amount to a demand to end all forms of assistance, including military training or the provision of defensive equipment, making it important to distinguish between financial and military support. An internal Nato opinion poll cited by Politico also showed that public support for Ukraine had fallen from 59% last year to 55% this year.
Janne Kuusela, Permanent Secretary at Finland's Ministry of Defence, warned that growing financial pressures on households could create more opportunities for populist rhetoric questioning how much governments should spend on Ukraine or their own national defence. The debate over Europe's security commitments is therefore increasingly becoming a domestic political contest over who should bear the cost, rather than simply a disagreement over the necessity of responding to the war.
At the heart of the challenge is a growing tension between Nato's long-term rearmament timetable and the electoral and fiscal pressures facing individual member states. At its 2025 summit in The Hague, the alliance agreed that members would allocate 5% of GDP to defence and security-related expenditure by 2035. Under the agreement, at least 3.5% is intended for core defence requirements, with up to 1.5% allocated to broader security-related areas, including critical infrastructure, civil preparedness, network protection and the defence industry. The commitment was reaffirmed at this year's Ankara summit, while Nato reported that core defence investment by its European members and Canada had risen by more than $139bn since the Hague agreement. The concern, therefore, is not necessarily that European rearmament is already in retreat, but whether the political support required to sustain it can endure.
Defence investment presents a particular political challenge because procurement programmes, expanded production facilities, military recruitment and ammunition stockpiles often require years of sustained funding before delivering tangible military capabilities. By contrast, higher taxes, inflation and pressure on public services are immediately felt by voters. Even where far-right parties remain outside government, their electoral influence could encourage established centrist parties to slow planned spending increases or adopt a more cautious approach towards joint EU defence projects. Such indirect political pressure may affect Europe's defence commitments before any formal change of government takes place.
These concerns are increasingly being voiced within Nato itself. One alliance official warned that European members were already facing the challenge of catching up with Russia, and that any interruption to defence funding could put military capabilities at risk. Another official cautioned that slower investment by major members such as France and Italy could have consequences across the alliance, undermining wider progress on strengthening Nato's defences. The warning comes amid heightened concern over Russian activities in Europe, with German intelligence authorities recently describing cyberattacks and acts of sabotage attributed to Moscow as part of a "shadow war" against the continent.
Nevertheless, treating all far-right opposition to increased defence spending as evidence of a pro-Russian position risks overlooking important differences between parties and countries. Their policies reflect varying national budget constraints, competing views on European integration and disagreements over the scale and nature of assistance to Ukraine. Even so, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has publicly argued that much of the pressure coming from the political right ultimately originates in Moscow. His criticism underscores how the debate is extending beyond national budgets to wider questions about Russian influence and the cohesion of the transatlantic alliance.
Ultimately, the success of Europe's rearmament drive will depend on more than how quickly governments can purchase weapons and expand their military capabilities. European leaders must also persuade voters why higher defence spending remains necessary despite inflation and fiscal pressures, and how investing in security today could reduce potentially greater costs in the future. While the fighting continues in Ukraine, another contest that could determine the future of Europe's defence commitments is increasingly taking shape at the ballot box.

high_priority_articles.title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls - BBC
high_priority_articles.summary: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls  BBCA year into Trump’s peace plan, Netanyahu stands in the way of rebuilding  The Washington PostIsrael’s ‘scorched-earth’ ceasefire in Gaza  Financial TimesIsrael kills or wounds Palestinian every 90 minutes in Gaza since ceasefire  Al Jazeera‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins  The Guardian
high_priority_articles.full_text:
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve Governor Chris Waller said in a speech Thursday that he expects the Fed will need to enact more interest rate hikes to bring down inflation faster if economic data comes in as he expects.
"If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2% goal," Waller said at the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye İstanbul Economic Forum. "But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur. The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time."
Waller noted that a convergence of factors has gelled into persistent inflationary forces, including hopes for a quick ending to the Middle East conflict and warnings that low inventories and damaged infrastructure could keep oil prices high through 2027. He also pointed out that the artificial intelligence build-out has significantly driven up high-tech consumer prices, and projections of its size have ballooned. Additionally, he said, continuing trade conflicts threaten new tariffs that could put upward pressure on inflation yet again.
"When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the FOMC's September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target," Waller said.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
Waller sees economic activity strengthening in the second half of this year, and says he's "not greatly concerned" that higher interest rates threaten to markedly slow down the economy.
"But I am concerned that the recent acceleration in inflation — after what soon will be five and a half years of it above the FOMC's target — will lead consumers, investors, and price-setting businesses to revise up their expectations for future inflation."
He noted that he sees the economy in roughly the same place as it was at the time of the Fed's policy meeting in mid-September.
"Overall, the new data reinforce my view that the labor market is stable and inflation is too high," he said. "For at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of our mandate."
Waller also made a point of sharing how he believes the Fed should communicate its interest rate expectations. He doesn't think choosing to say nothing or offering a strong indication of what the Fed will do is how the central bank should communicate. Rather, he believes an in-between approach of signaling the amount of rate hikes over some time interval, while not saying what the pace of hikes will be or how large they will be, would offer flexibility, while keeping the public informed.

Representatives from the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade) provided information and explanations on some of the reasons for the recent surge in electronics imports, along with solutions for directing and managing exports to further promote exports and control the trade deficit.
Three main reasons for the surge in electronics imports.
At the Ministry of Industry and Trade 's regular press conference for the third quarter of 2026, held on the afternoon of October 7, 2026, the import-export situation and the trade deficit were of great interest to many journalists.
Regarding the recent surge in imports, particularly of electronics, computers, components, and equipment, Ms. Trinh Thi Thu Hien, Deputy Director of the Import-Export Department, provided information and explanations on several contributing factors.

The second reason related to the increase in imports is the issue of inventory and stockpiling. high_priority_articles.title: France and Germany float ‘trade bazooka’ against China as the EU sends envoy to Beijing - Fortune
high_priority_articles.summary: France and Germany float ‘trade bazooka’ against China as the EU sends envoy to Beijing  Fortune
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach toward its second-largest trading partner.
The European Commission’s top trade envoy, Maroš Šefčovič, will be in Beijing Thursday for a two-day meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The goal is narrowing the EU’s 360 billion euro ($410 billion) trade deficit with China. Earlier this year, he gave Beijing a deadline of October to provide meaningful results in doing so.
Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China’s massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories. China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the U.S. raised tariffs.
In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China. On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for “economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets.”
Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that “Europe has economic power, it’s time we used it.”
EU options range from tariffs to a “trade bazooka”
Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels.
France’s High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30% tariffs on many of China’s exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency. Sales of German autos are plummeting in China, but China is also poised to gobble up market share in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies. There have already been mass layoffs at major manufacturers like Volkswagen.
A letter by France and Germany, a copy of which was seen by The Associated Press, called for a sweeping rethink of the EU’s China policy. Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc’s so-called “trade bazooka,” the Anti-Coercion Instrument. This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations.
Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy, has been less adversarial toward China in recent years. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years. Far-right and left-wing lawmakers from Ireland to Bulgaria formed an unusual coalition on Wednesday to vote against resolution calling for tougher China policies.
The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already hemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another “ China shock ” for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out.
The EU’s ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies, the bloc’s internal think tank.
Rühlig also said that European businesses and political leadership bear some blame.
“It’s clear that just protecting yourself from China is not the future,” Rühlig said. “But to have a chance of making yourself ready for future technologies and to remain competitive in the coming 15-20 years, you have to protect yourself.”
It is impossible to disengage completely with China as the EU did with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, Rühlig said, but there is robust momentum now to reset trade relations with Beijing.
“Where do we make ourselves independent or at least more diverse? And where do we still work with the Chinese?” Rühlig asked.
On Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his Greece visit called for Europe to strengthen its alliance with the U.S. as he urged Europe to “awaken from its long slumber.”
Rubio said that Europe and the U.S. are at “a crossroads” where actions taken now “will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.”
China is ready for a long trade dispute
This week in Beijing, when asked about the letter penned by France and Germany, a spokesperson at China’s Ministry of Commerce said that the countries should refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures.
“Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, and decoupling or cutting off supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.
China is the EU’s second-largest goods trading partner after the U.S., according to European Commission data. Chinese exports to the EU rose 15.3% in the first eight months of this year, according to China’s customs agency, while its imports from the EU rose 6.2%.
“The EU does not have the capacity to wage a trade war against China,” read an editorial last month in China’s state-run Global Times newspaper. “If it is truly determined to do so, then let it try.”
China’s exports to Europe, as well as Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa, expanded after U.S. tariffs went into effect last year, but it still booked a $1.2 trillion trade surplus globally in 2025. So far, China’s export machine has remained remarkably resilient despite U.S. tariffs and other trade restrictions, said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.
This past weekend, ahead of the meeting between Šefčovič and Wang, China launched an anti-dumping probe on EU exports of p-nitrotoluene, which is used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. The probe was initiated after Beijing warned last month that it would take retaliatory actions if the EU instituted tougher protectionist trade measures.
“China has been battle-tested by successive rounds of external pressure and, so far, has largely stared down attempts to force a change in course,” said Zenglein.
China’s economy has been largely driven by exports as domestic demand remains sluggish. The EU imports sizable amounts of Chinese lithium-ion batteries and hybrid electric vehicles, and Chinese carmakers are also expanding production capacity in Europe.
While China’s trade surplus has intensified concerns among its major trading partners, trade ties between the U.S. and China appear relatively stable following a summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Washington, wrote Bank of America economists, turning the attention to China-EU relations.
When it comes to negotiations with the EU, Chinese investment in Europe is likely to be among Beijing’s bargaining chips, Zenglein added, particularly as EU member states compete to attract capital, jobs, and new manufacturing projects.
___
Chan reported from Hong Kong.

high_priority_articles.title: China cautions France, Germany against protectionist moves ahead of EU trade talks - Asia News Network
high_priority_articles.summary: China cautions France, Germany against protectionist moves ahead of EU trade talks  Asia News Network
high_priority_articles.full_text:
LONDON – Ahead of high-level trade talks between China and the European Union later this week, Chinese officials and experts have warned France and Germany against resorting to protectionist measures, politicizing economic issues and framing them in terms of security.
The warning came after a letter jointly signed by French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to bolster the EU with a new trade diversification instrument and a new trade defense measure.
Reuters reported on Monday that the letter, together with an unofficial proposal paper, had been welcomed by the commission, which said it was a valuable contribution to the debate on geoeconomic risks and global imbalances, and aligned with Von der Leyen’s stance on competitiveness and her approach to EU trading partners.
Though the letter did not mention China, analysts said China was the most likely focus of the proposal as it was sent out before possible China-EU trade talks on Thursday.
A spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday that the ministry had taken note of the report and expressed hope that France and Germany, as major global economies, would uphold openness, cooperation and free trade, abide by World Trade Organization rules, and refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures at every turn. Still less should they politicize economic and trade issues under the garb of security concerns.
“They should avoid taking the wrong approach down the wrong path, which could ultimately backfire on themselves,” the spokesperson said.
The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU also issued a response opposing the reported proposal in its current form and calling for continued dialogue, consultation and a balanced approach to addressing trade concerns.
“At a particularly critical stage of the ongoing China-EU trade negotiations, we believe that introducing such a mechanism could increase uncertainty, undermine mutual trust and complicate efforts to achieve constructive and tangible outcomes,” said a spokesperson for the CCCEU.
In June, China and the EU held the first round of trade talks and established four workstreams covering trade and investment balancing, export controls, intellectual property rights and WTO reform.
The progress came against the backdrop of deep economic ties between the two sides, with bilateral trade exceeding $828 billion in 2025.
Michael Schumann, chairman of the board of the Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade of Germany, said German businesses are increasingly concerned about the political uncertainty surrounding the economic relationship between the two sides and expect a credible political signal that the EU and China want to manage their differences rather than escalate them.
“Companies need predictability,” said Schumann. They want fair competition and better market access, and want to preserve the enormous opportunities that continue to exist in China, he added.
“At the same time, Europe should avoid creating the impression that new economic instruments are an end in themselves. Strong instruments can have a role as a safeguard and as leverage in negotiations, but the objective must always be to create better and more balanced conditions for trade.”
He said the logic that every dispute must be answered with another restriction should be avoided. “Once retaliation becomes the dominant dynamic, businesses and consumers on both sides lose.”
Schumann regarded the talk of a “kill switch” in the current debate and reporting surrounding the Franco-German paper as irresponsible rhetoric.
“I have said repeatedly that language matters in international relations. Words can open doors, but they can also close them. Europe should defend its legitimate economic interests firmly, but we should not talk ourselves into a confrontation that neither side can benefit from,” he added.
Mark Logan, a London-based political risk consultant and former member of the British Parliament, said Europe should pay close attention to signs of greater engagement displayed at the recent China-United States summit and pursue more cooperation with China rather than engage in protectionist measures.
“European leaders must find a way to work with China and the new emerging centers of economic power by learning the most important ingredients for their success: technological innovation and entrepreneurialism,” said Logan.

high_priority_articles.title: Asim Munir wants to split Pakistan's four provinces into smaller states - India Today
high_priority_articles.summary: Asim Munir wants to split Pakistan's four provinces into smaller states  India TodayA selfish ploy to break up Pakistan  The EconomistA controversial new power grab in Pakistan  Hindustan TimesWhy is Pakistan debating new provinces, and what would it take to create them?  Moneycontrol.comPakistan's territorial restructuring creates fresh avenues for patronage: Report  www.thehawk.in
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Breaking up Pakistan's giant provinces could weaken alternative centres of power and make the country's administrative structure more responsive to the demands of the military establishment.
The biggest change to Pakistan's political map in decades could be under consideration. Pakistan is currently organised around four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. The Economist reports that army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir now wants to divide these large provinces into smaller states, potentially creating anywhere from 12 to 15 new provinces or even 160 smaller territories.
The proposal would amount to a fundamental overhaul of how power is organised across Pakistan. It would not simply change the names or boundaries on a map. Breaking up Pakistan's giant provinces could weaken alternative centres of power and make the country's administrative structure more responsive to the demands of the military establishment.
On paper, there is a straightforward case for restructuring Pakistan's provinces. The four existing provinces are vastly different in population and size. Punjab, the country's most populous province, has around 128 million people, or more than half of Pakistan's population. Balochistan, despite being the country's largest province by area, has only about 15 million residents.
Governing Punjab's enormous population has produced serious administrative problems. In rural areas, residents can travel for hours to access government services, while fewer than a quarter of Punjabis have reliable access to safe drinking water at home, according to the report.
Munir has argued that the provinces are simply too large to be governed effectively and that this contributes to Pakistan's poor performance.
Pakistan's problems are difficult to dispute. The country has struggled with weak growth, high inflation and punishing debt-servicing costs. But the causes run much deeper than the size of Pakistan's provinces.
ASIM MUNIR'S RISING INFLUENCE
The military has directly ruled Pakistan for more than two-fifths of the country's history, while elected governments have often operated under its shadow. The Economist argued that the military itself has contributed to many of the problems Munir says smaller provinces could solve. It noted the army's control over valuable land and businesses, as well as its large share of state resources.
That creates the contradiction surrounding the proposal.
If Pakistan's provincial governments are failing to deliver, breaking them into smaller units could be presented as an attempt to bring government closer to citizens. But if the new units are weaker and more dependent on the centre, the restructuring could also make it easier for the military establishment to exercise influence over them.
WHY PUNJAB AND SINDH MATTER
Pakistan's four provinces are not simply administrative divisions. They are also major political power bases. Punjab has traditionally been dominated by the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz, while Sindh remains the stronghold of the Pakistan Peoples Party.
Both provinces have provided alternative centres of political power even during periods of military rule. That makes the prospect of breaking them into smaller units politically significant.
The large provinces have acted as a counterweight to the central government precisely because of their political and electoral strength. Splitting them into smaller units could dilute that influence. The question, therefore, is not only whether smaller provinces would be easier to govern.
It is whether smaller provinces would also be easier for the centre to control.
THE IDEA IS NOT NEW
The proposal to reorganise Pakistan's administrative structure is not new. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has previously spoken about the need for a larger number of provinces and smaller administrative units, including the possibility of 12 to 15 provinces and up to 160 districts.
The proposal is emerging at a time when Munir has accumulated extraordinary grip over Pakistan's politics. Munir effectively rules Pakistan despite the existence of an elected government. He has strengthened his position by working with the PML-N and PPP while keeping Imran Khan, the leader of Pakistan's third major political force, in jail.
Khan's supporters have protested his imprisonment. Authorities have responded with crackdown on his movement.
That political backdrop makes the proposed restructuring difficult to separate from the wider struggle over power in Pakistan.
PAKISTAN IS ALREADY FACING UNREST IN KP
The debate over provincial restructuring comes as Pakistan is dealing with fresh political turmoil in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Thousands of supporters of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan began a march towards Islamabad earlier this week after talks between Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf and the government failed. The march began in KP, which is governed by Khan's party. The Pakistani government has deployed heavy security around Islamabad and vowed to prevent the protesters from entering the capital.
The march has put additional pressure on the relationship between the federal government and the PTI-led administration in KP, at a time when the province is also dealing with a serious militancy problem.
BALOCHISTAN AND POK ADD TO THE PRESSURE
Pakistan's political map is also being tested by unrest beyond the four provinces.
Balochistan has for years faced separatist violence over its so-called independence, resources and the role of Islamabad. Any attempt to divide the province would therefore involve highly sensitive questions about territory, resources and local political power.
Pakistan-occupied Kashmir has also remained an important source of discontent, with anger over governance, prices, taxation and economic conditions periodically spilling into protests. Together, these pressures underline how complicated any attempt to redraw Pakistan's internal structure would be.
There is a genuine administrative argument for smaller provinces. Pakistan has grown enormously since 1947, and some of its existing states are vast and difficult to govern. Against that backdrop, breaking four powerful provinces into smaller states would not simply redraw Pakistan's administrative map. It could redraw Pakistan's balance of power.

Gold Price Today, October 8: Gold prices traded largely unchanged on Thursday, October 8, hovering near the USD 4,100 mark after the release of the Federal Reserve's latest meeting minutes reinforced expectations of additional interest rate hikes later this year.
As of 6:05 AM IST, spot gold was trading nearly flat at USD 4,109.18 per ounce. The precious metal had slipped to a near two-month low in the previous session as investors reacted to the Fed's hawkish policy outlook. Spot silver also traded in a narrow range below the USD 60 per ounce mark.
In the domestic market, gold and silver futures were not trading at the time of writing. In the previous session, MCX Gold Futures settled at Rs 1,49,110 per 10 grams, while MCX Silver Futures ended at Rs 2,23,353 per kg.
Gold under pressure after hawkish Fed minutes
Bullion prices remained under pressure after the minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting signalled that policymakers remain inclined towards further monetary tightening.
Last month, the FOMC unanimously voted to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points, marking the first interest rate increase in more than three years.
"With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year-end," the minutes stated.
The hawkish tone reinforced market expectations for another rate hike in the coming months, weighing on sentiment across precious metals.
Strong dollar, rising bond yields weigh on bullion
Following the release of the Fed minutes, the US dollar and Treasury yields strengthened, limiting upside in gold prices.
The US Dollar Index remained above the 102 level, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield extended gains after touching fresh highs earlier in the session.
A stronger US dollar and higher bond yields typically act as headwinds for gold, as they increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion and make the precious metal more expensive for holders of other currencies.
Elevated crude oil prices fuel inflation concerns
Market participants also remained cautious amid persistent inflation concerns. Elevated crude oil prices have added to worries that inflation could remain higher for longer, prompting central banks to maintain a tighter monetary policy stance.
The rise in energy prices has strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve may have to keep rates elevated or even hike rates further during 2026.
According to the CME FedWatch Tool, markets are currently pricing in around an 80 per cent probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike at the December FOMC meeting.
Rising rate-hike expectations are generally negative for gold prices, as higher interest rates boost the appeal of interest-bearing assets while also supporting the US dollar.
Gold Price Outlook
Going forward, investors will closely monitor upcoming US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials for further clues on the trajectory of interest rates.
Key macroeconomic releases, including inflation, labour market and consumer spending data, are expected to influence expectations regarding future Fed policy decisions.
Meanwhile, geopolitical developments will remain on traders' radar. Any escalation in global tensions could impact energy markets, inflation expectations and safe-haven demand, potentially triggering fresh volatility in gold prices.
While gold continues to derive support from its status as a hedge against economic uncertainty, a stronger dollar, elevated bond yields and rising rate-hike expectations may continue to cap gains in the near term.
